rem:glossary-exact-pairing:
Remark Exact pairing. Exact pairing. Given objects X and Y in a monoidal category, an exact pairing consists of morphisms \varepsilon \colon X \otimes Y \to \mathbf{1} (evaluation) and \eta \colon \mathbf{1} \to Y \otimes X (coevaluation) satisfying the snake identities:

(\varepsilon \otimes \mathrm{id}_X) \circ (\mathrm{id}_X \otimes \eta) = \mathrm{id}_X, \qquad (\mathrm{id}_Y \otimes \varepsilon) \circ (\eta \otimes \mathrm{id}_Y) = \mathrm{id}_Y.

When an exact pairing exists, Y is a right dual of X, and X a left dual of Y.
rem:glossary-left-dual: Remark Left dual. Left dual. An object Y in a monoidal category has a left dual if there exists an object X and an exact pairing (X, Y).
rem:glossary-right-dual: Remark Right dual. Right dual. An object X in a monoidal category has a right dual if there exists an object Y and an exact pairing (X, Y).
rem:glossary-rigid-category: Remark Rigid category. Rigid category. A monoidal category in which every object has both a left dual and a right dual.
rem:glossary-pivotal-category:
Remark Pivotal category. Pivotal category. A rigid monoidal category equipped with a monoidal natural isomorphism \delta_X \colon X \xrightarrow{\sim} X^{\vee\vee} between each object and its double dual.

The pivotal structure is what makes a left trace definable alongside the right one: without \delta there is no way to close the left-hand loop back onto X, since evaluation lands on X^{\vee\vee}. A pivotal category in which the two traces then agree on every object is called spherical; pivotal alone does not force that agreement. The left quantum dimension, defined through the inverse braiding, is in general a different morphism from the right one, so sphericality is an additional hypothesis rather than a consequence of the pivotal structure.
rem:glossary-compact-closed-category: Remark Compact closed category. Compact closed category. A symmetric monoidal category that is also rigid. Since the braiding identifies X \otimes Y \cong Y \otimes X, left duals and right duals coincide.
rem:glossary-r-linear-category: Remark R-linear category. R-linear category. A category whose hom-sets carry the structure of R-modules (for a commutative ring R) such that composition is R-bilinear.
rem:glossary-no-quasi-zeros:
Remark Algebra without quasi-zeros. Let R be a commutative ring with unity and A an R-algebra. An element a \in A is a quasi-zero if

  bac = 0 \qquad \text{for all } b, c \in A \text{ not both } 1.

The algebra A is without quasi-zeros if no such element exists. Assume that R has no quasi-zeros. This ensures that leading-term decompositions are well-defined and the division algorithm terminates correctly. It guarantees that R-linear hom-spaces have no phantom morphisms annihilated by all compositions, making the Frobenius pairing non-degenerate.
rem:glossary-cemetery-group: Remark Cemetery group. Cemetery group. The cemetery group \mathcal{Z}_n \subset \mathcal{K}_n is the localising subcategory of graded projective KLR modules annihilated by the fibre functor \tau. It acts as a homological pruning filter on the Gröbner–Shirshov reduction engine. A state word that lands in \mathcal{Z}_n is buried: its image under any subsequent observation vanishes, allowing the computation branch to be dropped.
sec:glossary-geometry-intro: This section defines the geometric and topological terminology used throughout this paper.
rem:glossary-quantum-flatness:
Remark Quantum flatness. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with gauge group G_q = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) and connection \nabla on A. Let \mathrm{INN}(G_q) denote the inner-automorphism 2-group of G_q, with 2-form datum B \in \Omega^2(A) \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(A).

The connection \nabla is quantum flat if the curvature F_\nabla equals the 2-form datum:

  F_\nabla = B.

This is not an independent axiom. It is a derived consequence of the instanton condition combined with the simplicity constraint B \in \Gamma(\Lambda^+ H^* \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(P)):

\begin{equation}\label{eq:quantum-flatness-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  F_\nabla \ar[r, equal, "\text{instanton}"]
    \ar[dr, equal, "F_\nabla = B"']
  & F_\nabla^+ \ar[d, equal, "\text{simplicity}"] \\
  & B
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\text{(quantum flatness)}
\end{equation}

The instanton equation \star_q F_\nabla = F_\nabla forces self-dual curvature. The simplicity constraint restricts B = F_\nabla^+. Therefore F_\nabla = B. Quantum flatness encodes the condition that the 2-group gauge theory of \mathrm{INN}(G_q) admits no independent 2-connection. The ordinary connection fully determines the 2-form datum.
rem:glossary-reeb-gauge-group:
Remark The Reeb gauge group U_1(R). Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe over R with maximal torus T and Reeb derivation \xi. The Reeb gauge group is the R-group scheme

  U_1(R)  :=  T
  =  \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau|_{\langle V \rangle})

which is the maximal torus of the gauge group G. Over \mathbb{C}, this recovers U(1). Over a general commutative ring R, it is the multiplicative group of norm-one elements in the rank-one weight lattice.

The Reeb gauge group plays six simultaneous roles, all arising from T \subset G:

  1. Gauge group of the Reeb fibre. The projective line \mathbb{P}(V) = G/T is a principal U_1(R)-bundle. The fibre over each point is a copy of T acting by scalar multiplication on the weight spaces. The Reeb derivation \xi is the infinitesimal generator of this U_1(R)-action.
  2. Weight grading. The U_1(R)-action on \Omega^k(A) induces the weight decomposition \alpha = \alpha_H + \alpha_V: \alpha_H \in \ker(\iota_\xi) (weight 0) and \alpha_V (non-zero weight). The characters of U_1(R) label the weights.
  3. Contact structure. The contact affine chart U_\xi \subset \mathbb{P}(V) is the complement of the U_1(R)-fixed locus. The contact form \varTheta_A satisfies \varTheta_A(\xi) = 1 and \iota_\xi d\varTheta_A = 0, defining a connection on the U_1(R)-bundle.
  4. Commutative observation direction. In the adjoint bundle \mathrm{Ad}(J^1\mathcal{S}), the U_1(R)-direction is the Cartan subalgebra. It is the one direction in the colour fibre where intents commute: [\mathfrak{O}_1, \mathfrak{O}_2] = 0 when both act along \xi. Fermionic uncertainty lives in the remaining two directions.
  5. Longitudinal backbone. In the harmonic decomposition of H^1(\mathcal{S}_n, \mathrm{ad}\mathcal{S}_n), the U_1(R)-modes are the longitudinal backbone: steady-state flows aligned with the Reeb direction.
  6. Arrow of time. The Reeb flow \phi_t^q is the one-parameter subgroup generated by \xi. Under the braiding-induced ordering \prec_c, forward time is the direction of this flow.
rem:glossary-categorical-transport:
Remark Categorical transport equation. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with instanton \nabla and q-deformed exterior derivative d_q. The categorical transport equation for a section \psi \in \tau(J^1(A)) is

\begin{equation}\label{eq:categorical-transport}
  \hbar_q\pi_V(\nabla\psi) =  \hat{H}_q(\psi),
\end{equation}

where \hat{H}_q \colon \tau(J^1(A)) \to \tau(J^1(A)) is the q-Hamiltonian endomorphism \hat{H}_q = -\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar_q\Delta_q + V_q, with V_q the potential arising from the curvature F_\nabla. The following diagram encodes the transport:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:transport-cd}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \tau(J^1(A)) \ar[r, "\nabla"] \ar[d, "j^1"']
  & \tau(J^1(A)) \otimes \Omega^1 \ar[d, "\pi_V"] \\
  \tau(A) \ar[r, "\hat{H}_q"']
  & \tau(J^1(A))
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
rem:glossary-categorical-q-torsion-leaf:
Remark Categorical q-torsion leaf. A q-torsion leaf is a maximal sub-object L \hookrightarrow A such that:

  1. Horizontality: L \subset \ker(\pi_V) (all forms on L are horizontal).
  2. Flow invariance: \phi_t^q(L) = L for all t (the q-Reeb flow preserves L).
rem:glossary-descent: Remark Descent. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe and let \{A_n\}_{n \geq 0} be the recursive brane tower. The descent is the reverse traversal of the tower. Passage from level n to level n{-}1 applies the restriction morphism r_n \colon A_n = J^1(A_{n-1}) \to A_{n-1}. In the archimedean realisation, this restricts the connection and bundle to the base manifold M_{n-1}. The descent terminates in finitely many steps, bounded by \mathrm{Krulldim} Z(\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A)).
rem:glossary-s3-group:
Remark Symmetric group S_3. Imposing the involution relations \sigma_i^2=\mathrm{id} on the braid group B_3 yields the symmetric group S_3:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:s3-presentation}
  S_3
  =\bigl\langle s_1,s_2
     \big| s_1^2=s_2^2=(s_1 s_2)^3=\mathrm{id}\bigr\rangle.
\end{equation}
rem:glossary-q-bit:
Remark The q-bit: unit of q-deformed information. A q-bit is the natural unit of information in a QOU with substrate parameter q. It is the information generated by one application of the q-connection \nabla_q across a fibre, which corresponds to one crossing resolution in the Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_n(q) or one iteration of the quadratic map f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q) on the exceptional divisor.

Definition. One q-bit = \eta_q in classical natural units, where

  \eta_q =  \frac{2q - 1}{q^3}

is the operational entropy.

The two Hecke eigenvalues. The name "q-bit" reflects the Iwahori--Hecke algebra's two eigenvalues q (symmetric channel) and -q^{-1} (antisymmetric channel). At q = 1 the eigenvalues merge to \pm 1 and one q-bit equals one classical nat.

Values.

q \eta_q (q-bits = classical nats) Regime
1 1.000 Classical limit (one q-bit = one nat)
q_0 0.892 The observed universe
\varphi^2 0.327 Golden threshold
\infty 0 Big Bang (no information)

"It from q-bit." Wheeler's "it from bit" asserts that physics emerges from information. The QOU refines this: observable physics emerges from q-deformed information. The observability axiom forces every observable quantity to be a rational function of q. Each elementary process produces exactly one q-bit. The substrate parameter q controls non-commutativity.
rem:glossary-q-bit-skein: Remark One q-bit = one Skein operation. The q-bit–Skein identification of one q-bit with one Skein operation unifies several structures in this paper.
rem:glossary-distinguished-triangle: Remark Distinguished triangle. Distinguished triangle. In an additive category \mathbf{T} with a shift functor X \mapsto X[1], a triangle is a diagram X \to Y \to Z \to X[1]. A pretriangulated structure on \mathbf{T} singles out a class of distinguished triangles, closed under isomorphism and rotation, containing X \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}} X \to 0 \to X[1], such that every morphism X \to Y extends to a distinguished triangle, and satisfying the octahedral axiom; the distinguished triangles play the role that short exact sequences play in an abelian category, and a functor to an abelian category is homological when it sends them to long exact sequences.
rem:glossary-derived-category: Remark Derived category. Derived category. For an abelian category \mathbf{A}, the derived category D(\mathbf{A}) is the localisation of the category of cochain complexes in \mathbf{A} at the quasi-isomorphisms (the maps inducing isomorphisms on cohomology); equivalently, the localisation of the homotopy category of complexes at the same class. It is a triangulated category whose distinguished triangles come from short exact sequences of complexes. The bounded derived category D^{b}(\mathbf{A}) is the full subcategory of complexes with bounded cohomology, and D^{b}(X) for a variety X means D^{b} of coherent sheaves on X.
rem:glossary-dg-category: Remark Differential graded category. Differential graded category. A category enriched in cochain complexes over a commutative ring R: each hom-object \mathrm{Hom}(X, Y) is a complex of R-modules, composition is a chain map \mathrm{Hom}(Y, Z) \otimes \mathrm{Hom}(X, Y) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, Z), and identities are cycles of degree zero. Taking zeroth cohomology of every hom-complex gives an ordinary category, the homotopy category of the dg category; a dg category with one object is a dg algebra. Dg categories are the setting in which Hochschild homology of a category, and functoriality of Hochschild homology under derived functors, are defined without choices.
rem:glossary-fourier-mukai-transform: Remark Fourier–Mukai transform. Fourier–Mukai transform. For smooth projective varieties X, Y and an object K of D^{b}(X \times Y), the functor \Phi_{K} \colon D^{b}(X) \to D^{b}(Y), E \mapsto Rp_{Y*}\bigl(p_{X}^{*}E \otimes^{L} K\bigr): pull back along the projection to X, tensor with the kernel K, push forward along the projection to Y. By Orlov's theorem [orlov1997] every fully faithful exact functor between such categories is a Fourier–Mukai transform with a unique kernel; the name records that the transform with kernel the Poincaré bundle on an abelian variety and its dual is the analogue of the Fourier transform.
rem:glossary-observed-value:
Remark Observed spacetime value. Let \mathbf{r}_z, \mathbf{g}_z, \mathbf{b}_z be the color tube coordinates at a point of Bring's surface. The observed spacetime value is the element of \mathbb{A}^1 recovered from the color tube coordinates by the Vieta identity:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:observed-value}
  \mathbf{r}_z + \mathbf{g}_z + \mathbf{b}_z + 4z + 1 =  0.
\end{equation}

This identity defines the polynomial projection \pi_z \colon R_z \times G_z \times B_z \to \mathbb{A}^1, (\mathbf{r}_z, \mathbf{g}_z, \mathbf{b}_z) \mapsto z. At a branch point z_c where chiral sheets merge, the exceptional divisor is coordinatised by the limiting color vector. The observed spacetime value reads off z_c from the color data via the identity above, providing a coordinate on the exceptional \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}).

Archimedean specialisation. What follows sits on the archimedean side of the substrate wall. It invokes real- or complex-analytic constructs. Generic categorical identities remain valid over an abstract coefficient ring; only their archimedean realisation is specialised here.
rem:glossary-weierstrass-projection:
Remark Weierstrass projection \wp_q(z). Definition. Let \mathcal{E}_q be the Descartes elliptic curve with Weierstrass coefficients p(q), r(q), and let \Lambda_q \subset \mathbb{C} be the period lattice of \mathcal{E}_q. The Weierstrass projection is the meromorphic function \wp_q : \mathbb{C}/\Lambda_q \to \mathbb{P}^1 defined by

  \wp_q(z) =  \frac{1}{z^2}
  +  \sum_{\omega \in \Lambda_q \setminus \{0\}}
  \left(\frac{1}{(z - \omega)^2} - \frac{1}{\omega^2}\right).

Period lattice. The lattice \Lambda_q is spanned by the two fundamental periods \omega_1(q), \omega_2(q) obtained by integrating the holomorphic differential \mathrm{d}x / y over a basis of H_1(\mathcal{E}_q, \mathbb{Z}). The lattice modulus \tau_q = \omega_2(q)/\omega_1(q) satisfies \mathrm{Im}(\tau_q) > 0 and encodes the conformal class of \mathcal{E}_q.

Uniformisation. The map

  \mathbb{C}/\Lambda_q \xrightarrow{ \sim } \mathcal{E}_q,
  \qquad
  z  \longmapsto  [\wp_q(z) : \wp_q'(z) : 1]

is an isomorphism of Riemann surfaces. This exhibits \mathbb{C}/\Lambda_q as the universal cover of \mathcal{E}_q.

Differential equation. The function \wp_q satisfies

  \wp_q'(z)^2 =  4\wp_q(z)^3
  +  4p(q)\wp_q(z)
  +  4r(q),

which is the standard Weierstrass equation \wp'^2 = 4\wp^3 - g_2\wp - g_3 with invariants g_2(q) = -4p(q) and g_3(q) = -4r(q). The factor of 4 converts the short Weierstrass form to the classical \wp-function normalisation.

Regime table.

Regime q Lattice shape Physics
Classical q = 1 \Lambda_1 rectangular Degenerate curve \mathcal{E}_1; no crossing asymmetry
Physical substrate q \Lambda_q rhombic The observed universe; \mathcal{E}_q smooth, \Delta < 0
Deep quantum q \to \infty \Lambda_q \to hexagonal CM lattice; maximal symmetry

Notation convention. The symbol \wp is reserved for the Weierstrass elliptic function associated to \mathcal{E}_q. It is never repurposed. \wp(z) abbreviates \wp_q(z) when the dependence on q is clear.
